Isolate, tag, lock and prove dead before entering.
The new one fitted to the machine. Record it here, then open a new installation period.

Step "%s": the lower bound is above the upper bound, so no reading can ever pass.
A hold point not done or not passed — the order cannot be closed while one remains.
Step "%(ten)s": "%(gt)s" is not among the declared choices (%(ds)s).
A conclusion drawn from the reading and the criteria, not from the person marking their own work.
Work happens at a PLACE. Which equipment was there is derived from the installation history.
Dealt with during last week's service; the oil trace is preservative oil not yet wiped off.
Used when the material is not in the catalogue. A one-off urgent purchase usually is.
The person ticked PASS (or not done) while the reading says FAIL, or the other way round.
What was seen, where, and when. The more specific it is, the less the triager has to go back and ask.
Derived from the location and the planned date. Editable when a different component has to be named.
Copied from the plan. The person doing the work need not look it up, and the checker knows what to compare against.
Inside the nacelle and up the tower. It has its own file on training, harnesses and rescue at height.
Why that mechanism occurred: wrong tightening torque, too little lubrication, a design fault, a batch fault…
Order "%s" is already closed — attaching a step now means a step nobody will ever carry out.
A SUGGESTION, not a conclusion. The real mechanism of each failure is declared on the work order itself.
Skipping or botching this step ruins the whole job. The order CANNOT be closed while a hold point is open.
Used when the person doing the work has no account in the system — most contractor staff do not.
Crane hire, specialists, transport. Grouped together because these usually arrive on a single invoice.
Counts only the hold that is OPEN. Total waiting time across several holds needs a per-hold log — not built yet.
Record the MEASURED value beside the criteria. Without it, "pass" is only a word and cannot be checked afterwards.
Skipping or botching this step ruins the whole service. The order CANNOT be closed while a hold point is open.
The regulation requires the issuer to know the work in detail and the conditions for electrical safety.
Derived from the location: the equipment installed there. Editable when the request names a component inside.
Taken from the outage attached to this order. At a power plant this is usually far larger than the intervention cost.
Step "%s" requires a photo. It is declared as one where words are not enough — attach the photo, then record the result.
The vendor supplies it free of charge. The quantity and serial number still have to be recorded, because they are the evidence for the next warranty claim.
Counted from the planned finish date. While the order is unfinished it counts up to today — so it does not stand still and look as if it were still in time.
The old one removed from the machine. Record it here, then close its installation period — without that, a serialised asset is lost track of.
The REAL mechanism this time. A failure mode suggests a common mechanism, but the same mode can come from several.
The outage this work deals with. Leave it empty when the job can be done without stopping the machine — and many jobs can.
Labour, materials and subcontracting on the orders attached to this outage. Add the lost revenue to get the real cost.
Removed for overhaul and refitted, keeping its serial-number history. Gearbox, generator, blades and converter are of this kind.
For "Reading" fields. Give a lower and upper bound and the system concludes pass or fail ITSELF — nobody has to mark their own work.
Why that mechanism occurred: wrong tightening torque, too little lubrication, a design fault, a batch fault. Different from the failure mode and the mechanism.
A rejected request stays in the log. Say plainly why,\n                   so that the person who raised it can still be answered later.
Generated by the field app, unique to each submission. Send the same key again and the server returns the existing record instead of creating another.
Order "%s" does not say who bears the cost. Close it empty and the amount cannot enter a warranty claim or a claim against the contractor.
The number of steps whose READING falls outside the criteria. Different from the steps a person ticked as failed — the gap between the two numbers is what is worth looking at.
What was seen, where, and when. The more specific it is, the less the triager has to go back and ask — and going back to ask is where the request log jams most often.
From being raised until someone triages it. While untriaged it counts UP TO TODAY — so it does not stand still and look as if it were still in time.
This location has %d other untriaged requests. Several people reporting the same thing usually means it is real — consider merging them while triaging.
The person raising it marked this a safety risk.\n It has to surface whatever the queue looks like.
Still "in progress" while in fact nobody is working on it. Only by separating the two can it be measured: an order open 14 days rarely has someone working all 14.
Kept apart from urgency: a job may not be urgent in energy terms and still be a safety risk, and it has to surface whatever the queue looks like.
It has to be one of the declared choices. On the web this is a checked text field; the drop-down lives in the field app, where the work is actually entered.
Order "%(ten)s" still has a HOLD POINT that has not passed: %(buoc)s.\n\nFinish it and tick it, or record FAIL with a reason and open a corrective order — do not simply close the order and leave it.
Mandatory inspection is kept apart because its deadline is set by law rather than chosen: overrun it and the equipment has to be stopped, not merely a worse indicator.
Waiting for a crane and waiting for weather are REAL reasons in wind, not excuses: a blade change needs a crawler crane mobilised for a week, and the wind has to be below the permitted limit.
This column answers the most expensive question of all: what share of failures is caught BEFORE energy is lost. Condition monitoring only pays for itself when that share is clearly higher.
Step "%s" recorded as FAIL has to say what was wrong — enter the measured value or a note. A bare "fail" leaves whoever repairs it later with no idea where to start.
Urgency here is the urgency the person raising it feels —\n the priority on the order is set by the dispatcher afterwards,\n weighed against the rest of the work.
Group by location here to see where the field reports\n the same thing over and over and is brushed off every time.\n That is usually where something really is about to fail.
Intervention + energy lost. This is the figure used to justify investing in preventive maintenance — look at intervention cost alone and prevention always looks like money wasted.
A template can be attached to any order, including an\n unplanned repair — unlike the steps of a maintenance plan, which\n are tied to a cycle.

The share of intervention cost attributed to warranty or recoverable from the O&M contractor. It does NOT include energy lost — that follows the contract's availability regime, with its own formula and cap.
Empty means it is used for every category. Fill it in and it only appears on work orders of that component category — a blade's failure-mode list is of no use for a converter.
An outage with no order is NOT an error — a remote restart is a real stoppage with no maintenance action. But a LONG outage with no order is worth asking about.
Order "%s" is on hold with no reason recorded. This field is the only thing that tells a slow repair from waiting on an outside resource — leave it empty and every overdue order looks alike.
Closing the order reports back to each person who\n raised it. Without that, they stop raising things —\n and a whole detection channel is lost.

Work on electrical equipment requires a work permit or a work instruction under the electrical safety regulation. That is a DIFFERENT document from this work order; the field below records only its number, for cross-reference.
steps where the person disagrees with the reading: the number says one thing and the result field another. This is worth looking at before closing the order.
A request is the front door, unlike a work order: what to do\n is not yet known, nor who does it, nor whether it is worth doing.\n The dispatcher triages it, and only then does it become an order.

DIFFERENT from who carries it out. The manufacturer may send its own people while the owner still pays, once the warranty has run out; your own crew may do the work while the cost is recoverable from the contractor. Pre-filled from the outage if there is one, and editable.

Repeated work across many machines (changing a whole fleet of gearboxes, re-pitching every blade on a site): one order per machine, gathered under a parent order. Each machine has its own schedule, cost and failure history, so they must not be merged.

A work order is the document that authorises spending labour,\n materials and time. It does not replace a work permit — the electrical\n safety document is still issued separately by an authorised person.
Response overdue. The clock here measures the time\n to triage, not the time to finish — so that\n the request log does not rot in silence.

This screen answers the question where the money and the time\n are stuck. An order open 14 days rarely has someone working all 14\n — most of it is waiting for materials, for a crane, or for weather.

Step "%(ten)s": measured %(do)s%(dv)s against criteria %(tc)s — it cannot be recorded as PASS.\n\nIf the reading is right, record FAIL and open a corrective order. If the criteria are wrong, fix them on the plan or the form template, not here.

Order "%(ten)s" says a failure occurred but no failure mode is chosen.\n\nClose the order with this empty and that failure never enters the reliability statistics — and there is no recovering it, because whoever knew has moved on to other work.

ENTERED BY HAND, not inferred from whether a work order exists. Many stoppages need only a remote restart: a stoppage, no failure. Planned maintenance is the other way round. Infer this field wrongly and MTBF is wholly wrong — wrong in the flattering direction.

Rejecting request "%s" requires a reason. A rejected request stays in the log precisely so that the question "how many times has the field reported this, and why was it brushed off every time" can be answered later — without a reason that question is meaningless.

Waiting for a crane and waiting for weather are REAL
                                reasons in wind: a blade change needs a crawler
                                crane mobilised for a week, and the wind has to
                                be below the permitted limit.
A rejected request stays in the log. That is the only way to answer later the question "how many times has the field reported this, and why was it brushed off every time".

Whoever does the work is not whoever pays. The manufacturer may send its own people while the owner still pays, once the warranty has run out; your own crew may do the work while the cost is recoverable from the contractor.
An outage with no work order is not an error — a remote restart is a real stoppage with no maintenance action at all. But a LONG outage with no order is worth asking about.

A failure mode is what can be observed (oil leak, overheating, vibration above threshold). A failure mechanism is the physical process behind it (fatigue, wear, corrosion). The root cause is why that mechanism occurred — declared on each work order, not here.

Order "%(ten)s" says a permit or work instruction is required but no number is recorded.\n\nUnder the electrical safety regulation, work on electrical equipment requires a work permit or a work instruction issued by an authorised person. This work order does NOT replace that document — enter the permit number, or untick "a permit or work instruction is required" if the work does not touch electrical equipment.

Replacing a rotable component means taking the old one out and fitting a new one, both carrying their own serial numbers. Record only a quantity and in a few years nobody knows which one is in the machine — which is exactly the question a warranty claim turns on.

Declare a lower and upper bound for a reading field and the system concludes itself whether it passes, and will not allow a Pass tick when the reading is outside the criteria. Without them the checklist is just a signed sheet of paper moved onto a screen.

This order currently says no failure occurred. Most stoppages need only a remote restart, and there really was no failure. But this field has to be entered by hand — inferring it from whether a work order exists makes the reliability statistics wrong in the flattering direction.

This work order is NOT a work permit. A work permit and a work instruction are two electrical safety documents defined by regulation (clause 3.8, QCVN 25:2025/BCT) and issued by an authorised person. The field below records only the number, to cross-reference the two files.

Total real cost = intervention + energy lost. Materials and labour are the visible part; at a power plant most of the money sits in the energy that could not be generated while the machine was down. Look at intervention cost alone and preventive maintenance always looks like money wasted.
Recoverable cost does not include energy lost — that follows the contract's availability regime, with its own formula and cap.
